name: SIMDMatrixAlgorithm
language: x86-64 NASM assembly with C and C++ drivers
baseline: scalar C and scalar C++ matrix multiply compiled with gcc -O3
claimed_speedup: README table: scalar C ~0.6 s (<1 GFLOP/s); scalar C++ ~1.3 s; NASM XMM (SSE, 2x unroll) ~0.29 s (~10 GFLOP/s); NASM YMM (AVX, 4x unroll) ~0.0098 s (~28 GFLOP/s), about 60x versus scalar C (derived); hybrid C+ASM and C++ +ASM ~0.010 to 0.020 s.
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX/FMA only; fixed unrolling; single-precision square matrices.
caveats: Gap above 50x, so tier capped at C: the baseline is a naive scalar triple loop that stays unvectorized and uncached despite -O3 -mavx -mfma, so the gap reflects missing blocking and vectorization in the baseline, not asm versus well-optimized compiler output. GFLOP/s and CPI columns have no methodology. README mentions AVX-512 gains of about 30x with no zmm build or data (and the Ryzen 5 5600X has no AVX-512).
found_via: WebSearch 'github README hand-written assembly implementation benchmark table versus portable C compiled with gcc -O3'

verification.tier_reason: The README table does compare scalar C/C++ with the NASM XMM/YMM and hybrid kernels on a named CPU (Ryzen 5 5600X) with stated gcc flags. However, the timed kernels produce wrong results, there is no correctness check, and the table contradicts itself, so the numbers carry no usable evidence. If the entry is kept, list it as D.
verification.notes: Reject per the stb-zip and fast_resize precedents (the fast path computes a different result): every timed asm path miscomputes the product (wrong M2 stride, lane-dropping horizontal add, results never stored, overlapping hybrid loads), and the README table contradicts itself (XMM 0.29 s labelled ~10 GFLOP/s; an AVX-512 claim with no zmm code on a Zen 3 CPU). If the orchestrator prefers keep-and-document, keep it at D with these shortcomings: 0-star student project, MIT, last commit 2025-10-14 (active).
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence: the measured kernels compute wrong answers (M2 rows read 1952 bytes apart instead of 2048, vhaddps drops the upper 128-bit lane, NASM results are never stored, the hybrid C ymm loads overlap at 16-byte offsets); the table contradicts itself (XMM 0.29 s labelled about 10 GFLOP/s; an AVX-512 30x claim with no zmm code on a Zen 3); the C++ baseline is double and copied by value. stb-zip and fast_resize precedent.
